meta.beh: Aggression toward staff: forceful contact of hand, foot, or head with an adult — audible on contact or leaving a visible mark.
meta.agree: The teacher, the aide and the SLP each put it in work he is left to do on his own, and each named an adult stepping away as what sets it off (the teacher: “It is the leaving him that does it, not the worksheet”). All three said it is least likely when an adult is with him (the aide: when two adults are in the room), and the student said he has the fewest problems when Miss A sits by him. All three described the same sequence afterwards: the work is taken away, stops or pauses, and an adult comes back to him or talks him down. The teacher and the aide both described a loud protest and pushing the materials first.
meta.disagree: They differ on function: the teacher said escape, the aide escape or getting the aide back, and the SLP escape with an attention component that could not be separated. What they describe setting it off and following it fits either. The SLP described a quiet, still period before it rather than a protest. The parent reported it at home when the tablet is ended or refused, and said the tablet is sometimes given back. That may be a real difference in conditions rather than a contradiction (the home routine has few independent academic demands), and it leaves open a separate function at home, recorded on Form FS-1 as cannot be ruled out.
meta.hyp: On informant report only (tier 4): at school, escape from work he is left to do on his own, the return of adult attention, or both together; in every school account an adult moving away sets it off, and the work stopping with the adult coming back follows it. At home, access to the tablet. Hypotheses to test, not identified functions.
meta.next: Direct observation at school: conditional probabilities on Form ABC-1, with the work stopping and the adult returning recorded as separate consequences, and the temporal pattern on Form SP-1 (the independent blocks, the afternoon). The two consequences arrive together in every account, so observation may not separate them; a functional analysis on Form EA-1 would test escape and adult attention in separate conditions, or together as the respondents describe them. Home was not observed, so nothing here extends to it.

ans.0_14: He knows when he has done it. He will come and find me afterwards.

ans.1_12: Sitting beside him. Breaking the work into two-minute pieces. Letting him choose the order.
ans.1_13: A way for him to ask for a break that we will actually honour, and the staffing to honour it.

ans.2_3: Most days in the afternoon block. Rarely in the morning.
ans.2_4: Mornings, when there are two of us in the room.
ans.2_5: Afternoon writing, when I am covering two students.
ans.2_6: Me stepping away. He is fine while I am there.

ans.2_11: I have tried giving him a break when he asks nicely, but he does not ask.

ans.2_13: A second adult in the afternoon, honestly.

ans.3_3: Twice in the six sessions I have seen him this term.
